result:
**Solution A is refuted.** Its uniform-weight lower bound 31/66 ≈ 0.4697 is valid, but the claimed upper bound fails. Its "parametric analysis" only checks one family of weight vectors and then asserts the uniform case is worst without proof. A better adversary exists.

**Solution B's answer is also too small**, but it is much closer to the truth and uses the right idea. With identical people, the selector only chooses integer counts n_c with sum 2025, and a color of weight w can hold at most ⌊T/w⌋ people when the max load is T. Take the 66 weights so that the allowed counts are m_c = 31 for 44 colors and m_c = 30 for 22 colors. That gives total capacity 44·31 + 22·30 = 2024 < 2025, so the selector cannot keep every load at or below T.

Such weights exist when T < 1/(44/32 + 22/31) = 248/517. The condition is that the interval lower bounds sum to less than 1 (which holds exactly when T < 248/517) and the upper bounds sum to at least 1 (which holds since 44/31 + 22/30 > 1/T). So C ≥ 248/517 ≈ 0.479691.

B's value 992/2069 ≈ 0.479458 is strictly smaller than 248/517, so B's maximum is wrong. B only considered the (p,q) = (32,31) case and missed the (31,30) configuration. Its Cauchy–Schwarz bound for three or more groups is also asserted without justification.

Neither answer is correct. Both are refuted by explicit constructions, but B is far closer to the true value and is built on the correct integrality-based framework, while A's value is well below a verified lower bound.

WINNER: B
